# Software Development Plan

## Purpose and Scope

The Software Development Plan (SDP) describes the project-level approach for
planning, developing, controlling, integrating, verifying, releasing, and
maintaining software for the Next-Generation Ground-based Solar Observing
Network (ngGONG).

For the Conceptual Design Review (CoDR), this document establishes the intended
software development framework and identifies areas where detailed standards,
tools, and procedures will be defined as the project matures.
Over time, this plan is expected to evolve into a working standard for ngGONG
software teams.

This plan applies to ngGONG software delivered under Work Breakdown Structure
(WBS) 9.0, High Level Software and Controls, and WBS 10.0, Data Management
System.
It describes software practices that are expected to be common across High
Level Software, Controls, and the Data Management System, including requirements
traceability, development workflow, configuration management, review, build,
integration, verification, release, and maintenance.

Where High Level Software and Controls, the Data Management System, or other
software areas require different tools or detailed procedures, those details may
be defined in subordinate standards, repository-specific documentation,
interface control documents, test plans, deployment procedures, or operations
procedures.

This plan does not define project-level processes for document control, risk
management, project reporting, budgeting, scheduling, or formal change control.
Those processes are managed through ngGONG project-level systems engineering,
project management, configuration management, and risk management plans.
The software team participates in those processes where software work products,
risks, changes, progress, or verification evidence are involved.

This plan also does not define the detailed software architecture, subsystem
designs, interface specifications, coding standards, cybersecurity
implementation, deployment topology, test procedures, or operations runbooks.
Those artifacts are maintained separately.
This plan identifies where such artifacts are needed and describes how they fit
into the overall software development process.

## Software Organization and Responsibilities

ngGONG software is currently developed and planned by a small core team covering
WBS 9.0, High Level Software and Controls, and WBS 10.0, Data Management System.
During early design, one person may cover multiple software functions, including
planning, technical direction, implementation, interface coordination,
integration, verification, release planning, and maintenance planning.

As the project matures, software responsibilities will be refined to reflect
staffing, contractor scope, subsystem ownership, and operational needs.
Contractor-delivered software packages are expected to follow applicable ngGONG
software practices and to have an assigned ngGONG technical point of contact or
software owner.

Coordination across the WBS 9.0 and WBS 10.0 boundary is the responsibility of
the applicable software leads.
Project-level authority for staffing, budget, formal change control, risk
management, document control, and project reporting is defined outside this
plan.

## Software Development Life Cycle

ngGONG software development will use an iterative and incremental life cycle.
During early design, the life cycle will emphasize requirements definition,
architecture, interface definition, risk-reduction prototypes, simulations, and
development infrastructure.
Prototypes will be used to evaluate uncertain or high-impact technical areas
before the project commits to detailed designs or implementation patterns.
Early development infrastructure will include the build, test, integration, and
deployment mechanisms needed to support later implementation work.
As the project matures, the emphasis will shift toward implementation,
integration, verification evidence, release control, deployment readiness, and
operations support.

The expected development flow is requirements, design, implementation, review,
build, integration, verification, release, deployment, and feedback from test,
commissioning, and operations.
The flow is not expected to be strictly linear.
Design decisions, test results, defects, interface changes, and operational
feedback may cause earlier work to be revisited.

ngGONG intends to use a Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment
(CI/CD)-informed development model in which software is built, tested, and
integrated frequently.
Continuous integration will be used to detect defects, interface changes, and
integration problems early.
Deployment automation will be used where appropriate, but promotion to site and
operational environments will remain controlled by project and operations
readiness criteria.

Software integration will occur early and repeatedly, especially where behavior
crosses the WBS 9.0 and WBS 10.0 boundary.
Simulators, test harnesses, and representative data flows are part of the
development life cycle and are expected to mature with the delivered software.

## Requirements Management and Traceability

Software requirements define the behavior and constraints that ngGONG software
must satisfy.
They may include functional behavior, interfaces, data products, timing,
performance, reliability, observability, deployment, maintainability, and
operations-support needs.

Software requirements will be derived from the ngGONG Operational Concept
Definition, Operational Architecture Document, Science Requirements, Instrument
Science Requirements, system and subsystem Design Requirements Documents
(DRDs), interface definitions, and operations needs.
Additional derived requirements may be identified through design work,
prototypes, integration planning, verification planning, and externally
developed software.

Software requirements will use stable identifiers so that related software work
can reference them.
Where applicable, issues, design artifacts, pull requests, code changes, tests,
release records, and verification evidence will reference the requirements they
satisfy or affect.
The project has not yet selected the final tooling or traceability schema, but
the software process will preserve links from requirements through
implementation and verification.
The level of traceability should match the risk and importance of the software
being changed.

Each software requirement should have an identified verification approach.
Verification may be performed by automated test, integration test, analysis,
inspection, demonstration, or operational acceptance, depending on the
requirement.
Where practical, automated tests should be used to support repeatable
requirement verification and regression testing.

Traceability is especially important where behavior crosses software subsystem
or hardware-control boundaries.
This includes interfaces between High Level Software and Controls, where
high-level software interacts with low-level programmable logic controller (PLC)
and hardware control systems, and interfaces between High Level Software,
Controls, and the Data Management System, where data, metadata, status, and
operational context are exchanged.
These cross-boundary behaviors must be traceable to the requirements and
verification evidence that govern them.

Externally developed software may be produced through different contracting
models, including staff augmentation, prototype studies, configured products, or
delivered software packages.
For software that becomes part of ngGONG, the responsible ngGONG software owner
must ensure that expectations, interfaces, acceptance criteria, delivered
artifacts, and maintenance responsibilities are clear before the software is
accepted.

## Interfaces, Architecture, and Design

Interfaces will be defined in forms that can be reviewed, version controlled,
and tested.
Where practical, ngGONG will use repository-controlled schemas, Protocol Buffer
definitions, interface definition files, data models, or API specifications as
the authoritative interface definition.
The repository that owns an interface definition should produce the generated
artifacts needed by both producers and consumers.
Prose interface control documents may still be used, but they should explain
intent, ownership, compatibility expectations, and operational assumptions
rather than duplicate machine-readable definitions.

The interface between High Level Software and Controls is a major design
boundary.
It includes commands, state models, telemetry, alarms, timing behavior,
interlocks, fault handling, and recovery behavior across the boundary between
high-level software and low-level Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) and
hardware control systems.
The interfaces between High Level Software, Controls, and the Data Management
System are also controlled design boundaries, especially for data products,
metadata, provenance, transfer status, and reduction context.

Design decisions that affect more than one team or subsystem will be captured in
a durable form, such as repository documentation, interface definitions, or
architecture decision records.
Simulators, test harnesses, and representative data flows may be developed as
part of the design when hardware, site systems, or Data Management System
services are not yet available.

## Development Environment and Tooling

ngGONG will define development environment and tooling expectations as the
software architecture and implementation technologies mature.
At this stage, the intent is to standardize where practical while allowing High
Level Software, Controls, and the Data Management System to use tools that fit
their technical needs.

Each software repository should document the tools and environment needed to
build, test, and run the software it contains.
This may include compilers, runtimes, package managers, test tools, simulators,
configuration files, environment variables, credentials, and external services.
The goal is that a new developer, contractor, or reviewer can reproduce the
development setup without relying on undocumented local knowledge.

Tooling choices should support repeatable build, test, static analysis,
packaging, deployment, and integration activities where practical.
Scripted, containerized, or otherwise reproducible development environments may
be used when they reduce setup drift, improve continuous integration, or make
contractor handoff more reliable.

## Source and Configuration Management

ngGONG will use GitHub as the primary source-control platform for delivered
software.
Software repositories should be maintained under the
[ngGONG GitHub organization](https://github.com/nggong) unless a specific
exception is needed.

Repository contents are controlled software artifacts.
This includes source code, tests, build definitions, interface definitions,
configuration schemas, deployment definitions, scripts, and repository
documentation needed to build, verify, deploy, or maintain the software.
Repositories should preserve enough dependency, build, and configuration
information to recreate released software versions.

ngGONG will use a multi-repository strategy where repository boundaries reflect
ownership, release cadence, deployment scope, and interface responsibility.
Shared interface definitions, common schemas, deployment definitions, and
reusable integration tooling should be maintained in repositories with clear
ownership and compatibility controls.
Each repository should have an accountable ngGONG software owner or lead.

Normal development should use a trunk-based workflow with short-lived branches.
The primary branch should be protected from direct commits.
Changes that affect delivered software, interfaces, tests, deployment behavior,
or operational behavior should be merged through pull requests or an equivalent
reviewed-change mechanism after required automated checks pass.

Controlled versions of software and interface definitions should be identifiable
by tags, releases, commit secure hash algorithm (SHA) values, or equivalent
version identifiers.
Changes should reference related requirements, issues, defects, interface
changes, releases, or deployments where applicable.
Generated artifacts should be excluded from source control unless there is a
clear reproducibility, delivery, review, or operational reason to include them.

## Coding Standards and Review Practices

ngGONG will define coding standards by repository or technology area as
implementation languages, frameworks, and runtime environments are selected.
Where practical, repositories should use established external standards rather
than project-specific style rules.
Google style guides may be used as baseline references where they fit the
selected language or ecosystem.

Coding standards should support readable, maintainable, testable software that
can be operated and modified over the lifetime of ngGONG.
Repository conventions should identify formatting, naming, static analysis,
linting, dependency-management, documentation, and test expectations that apply
to the software in that repository.

Changes that affect delivered software, interfaces, tests, deployment behavior,
or operational behavior should be reviewed before merge.
Review depth should match the risk and impact of the change.
Small internal changes may need only a lightweight review, while changes to
interfaces, safety-relevant behavior, deployment mechanisms, data products, or
operations workflows require more careful review.

Code review should evaluate correctness, maintainability, test coverage,
interface impact, operational impact, and consistency with repository
conventions.
Automated checks should be used where practical for formatting, linting, static
analysis, dependency checks, and test execution.
Human review remains responsible for design judgment, operational judgment, and
risks that automated tools cannot reliably assess.
AI-assisted review may be used when helpful, but it does not replace accountable
human review.

Known exceptions to coding standards or review expectations should be documented
where they affect delivered software, interfaces, operations, or long-term
maintenance.
New or modified tests should be included where practical for changed behavior,
fixed defects, and interface changes.

## Build, Integration, and Continuous Integration

Build, integration, and continuous integration practices provide the mechanism
for building ngGONG software repeatably, integrating software early, and
detecting defects before they accumulate.
Each delivered software repository should provide documented build instructions
and should build from version-controlled source and declared dependencies.

Controlled builds should record or preserve the source commit, dependency
versions, build tools, build configuration, and build environment needed to
reproduce the build.
This information may be stored in the repository, continuous integration (CI)
records, artifact metadata, or release records, depending on the repository and
release model.
Build outputs should be traceable to the source version, dependency versions,
and build process that produced them.
Generated interface artifacts should normally be treated as build products
unless there is a clear reason to maintain them in source control.

Continuous integration should be used for pull requests and primary-branch
changes where practical.
CI checks should match the needs of the repository and may include compilation,
unit tests, linting, static analysis, packaging, schema validation, and interface
compatibility checks.
Fast checks should be suitable for routine pull requests.
More expensive integration tests may run on a schedule, on release candidates,
or in dedicated integration contexts.

Interface definitions are build inputs and should be checked for compatibility
with affected producers and consumers where practical.
Integration should begin before all delivered hardware, site systems, or Data
Management System services are available.
Simulators, emulators, test harnesses, representative data, and mocked services
may be used to support early integration.

Build, integration, and continuous integration practices should support
integration across High Level Software, Controls, and the Data Management
System, especially where command behavior, state transitions, Programmable Logic
Controller (PLC) and hardware-control boundaries, telemetry, alarms, metadata,
provenance, and data transfer are involved.
CI results provide evidence that automated checks passed, but they do not by
themselves approve software for site or operational deployment.

## Verification and Validation

Software verification provides evidence that ngGONG software satisfies its
allocated requirements.
Software validation provides evidence that the software supports the intended
operational and science use when integrated into the ngGONG system.
This section describes the software evidence strategy; detailed test procedures,
acceptance criteria, commissioning plans, and operations validation plans are
maintained separately.

Each software requirement should have an identified verification method.
Verification methods may include automated test, integration test, analysis,
inspection, demonstration, or operational acceptance.
The depth of verification should match the risk and impact of the requirement.
Where practical, automated tests should be used for repeatable behavior,
interface compatibility, regression testing, data validation, and failure
handling.

Software verification will use multiple test levels where applicable, including
unit, integration, system, interface, performance, fault and recovery, and
acceptance testing.
Early verification may use prototypes, simulations, emulators, representative
data, mocked services, and test harnesses before all delivered hardware, station
systems, or Data Management System services are available.
Repository-specific test strategies may be used, but cross-subsystem behavior
should be verified in representative integration contexts.

Verification is especially important where behavior crosses software subsystem
or hardware-control boundaries.
High Level Software and Controls verification should cover commands, state
transitions, telemetry, alarms, timing behavior, interlocks, fault handling, and
recovery behavior across the boundary between high-level software and low-level
Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) and hardware control systems.
Interfaces between High Level Software, Controls, and the Data Management
System should be verified for data products, metadata, provenance, transfer
status, completeness, integrity, and reduction context.

Verification evidence should be traceable to requirements, issues, builds,
releases, and test results where applicable.
Continuous integration results may provide part of this evidence, but passing
automated checks alone does not necessarily establish readiness for acceptance,
site deployment, or operations.
Regression tests should be added for fixed defects where practical.

## Release and Deployment Management

ngGONG release and deployment practices will identify what software was built,
what combination of artifacts was qualified, what release is approved for
deployment, and what release is installed in each environment or station.
Release and deployment details may differ across High Level Software, Controls,
and the Data Management System because those systems have different runtime
models, hardware dependencies, operational constraints, and deployment
mechanisms.

Release processes should separate build identity, artifact identity, release
identity, and deployment state.
A build identifies the output of one component build.
An artifact identifies immutable content, such as a container image digest or
published package.
A release identifies a tested composition of artifacts and deployment
configuration.
Deployment state identifies the release approved or installed for a specific
environment, channel, or station.

Released software should be traceable to source revisions, dependency versions,
build records, configuration revisions, verification evidence, and deployment
records.
Promotion to an operational environment is a controlled deployment decision; it
is not the same as passing continuous integration or publishing a build
artifact.

### Controls

The release and deployment strategy for Controls is not yet defined.
Controls deployment may require different practices because it includes
low-level Programmable Logic Controller (PLC), hardware-control, safety,
interlock, vendor-tool, and station-maintenance constraints.
Controls-specific release practices will be defined with the Controls design,
hardware integration approach, and operations procedures.

### DMS

The release and deployment strategy for the Data Management System (DMS) is not
yet defined.
DMS deployment may require different practices because it includes data
pipelines, storage systems, processing environments, data-product compatibility,
and operational data retention concerns.
DMS-specific release practices will be defined with the DMS architecture,
pipeline design, and operations model.
### HLS - OCS

The release and deployment strategy for the High Level Software (HLS)
Observatory Control System (OCS) is not yet defined.
The OCS strategy will be developed as the OCS architecture, deployment model,
operations role, and interface responsibilities mature.

### HLS - SCS

The HLS Site Control System (SCS) release strategy uses immutable component
artifacts and immutable system release manifests.
Component builds produce artifacts such as container images or published
packages.
Human-readable tags or channels may be used for navigation, but deployment
decisions should resolve to immutable artifact identifiers.

Each deployable SCS component should have a continuous integration pipeline that
builds the component, runs the applicable automated checks, verifies relevant
interfaces, publishes the artifact, and records the immutable artifact identity.
A component-level candidate means that the component passed its own checks and
is eligible for inclusion in an SCS release candidate.
It does not mean that the component has passed SCS system qualification or is
approved for production deployment.

An SCS deployment repository should define deployment configuration and compose
SCS release candidates.
The release-composition process should resolve each required component to an
immutable artifact identity, identify the deployment-configuration revision,
generate an immutable release manifest, assign a unique SCS release identifier,
and archive the manifest before deployment or qualification.
The process should fail rather than create an incomplete release when required
components, configuration, or provenance cannot be resolved.

The SCS release manifest is the system-level release artifact.
It records the exact component artifacts and deployment configuration that were
qualified.
At minimum, the manifest should identify the SCS release, the creating pipeline
or process, the deployment repository revision, component artifact identities,
component source revisions, configuration revisions, applicable schema or
migration levels, and available provenance records.
The manifest should be machine-validated.

SCS qualification should test the exact release manifest under evaluation.
New component candidates published while qualification is in progress should not
change the release being tested.
If qualification succeeds, an authorized promotion process may advance the
applicable deployment channel to the qualified release.
Promotion should use the same manifest and artifact identities that passed
qualification; it should not rebuild component artifacts or create a replacement
manifest.

SCS deployment channels are mutable pointers to immutable release manifests.
A channel may represent a candidate release, a production release, or a
station-specific approved release.
Stations should deploy only the release approved for their applicable channel
and should not deploy from component-level candidate tags, production tags, or
latest tags.
Before deploying, a station should confirm that the selected release remains
approved and has not been revoked.

Promotion, revocation, and rollback are separate operations.
Promotion advances a channel to a qualified release.
Revocation prevents future deployment of a defective or withdrawn release.
Rollback changes desired or installed state to a prior known-good release when
that is operationally safe.
Revoked release manifests, artifacts, evidence, and deployment history should be
retained rather than modified or deleted.

Rollback should not be assumed to be safe for stateful components.
Database migrations, persisted data formats, protocol state, and controller
configuration may require a forward fix or a specific recovery procedure.
Stateful SCS components should declare whether rollback is supported, requires
state restoration, or is not supported for a given release transition.

SCS release, channel, qualification, revocation, rollback, and station
deployment records should use stable identifiers.
The records should make it possible to determine which source revisions produced
each artifact, which artifacts formed each release, which configuration was
applied, which tests qualified the release, who or what promoted or revoked it,
and which release each station installed.

## Defect and Issue Management

ngGONG software issues will be tracked in a common issue-tracking system where
practical.
The project has not yet selected the final software issue-tracking tool.
Candidate tools include GitHub Issues and Atlassian Jira.
The selected approach should support traceability across software work,
requirements, pull requests, builds, releases, verification evidence, and
deployment records.

Software issue tracking should include defects, enhancement requests, technical
tasks, interface changes, test failures, integration problems, and operational
software problems.
Issues should contain enough information to reproduce, evaluate, prioritize,
assign, and close the work.
Each issue should identify the affected subsystem, repository, interface,
deployment context, or test environment where applicable.

Defects should be classified by severity and impact.
Relevant impact areas include operations, data products, safety or
hardware-control behavior, interfaces, integration, deployment, and maintenance.
Each issue should have an accountable software owner or lead for triage and
resolution.
Cross-subsystem issues should be triaged with the affected leads, especially
where behavior crosses the High Level Software and Controls boundary or the
High Level Software, Controls, and Data Management System boundary.

Fixed defects should include regression tests or other verification evidence
where practical.
Known limitations, accepted defects, deferred fixes, and waivers should be
recorded when they affect delivered software, operations, interfaces, or
long-term maintenance.
Defect history should be preserved well enough to support release decisions,
operational troubleshooting, and maintenance planning.

Software defects should be escalated into project-level risk management,
configuration management, or change-control processes when their impact warrants
project-level handling.
Recurring or systemic defects should be treated as evidence that requirements,
design, tests, tooling, or operational procedures may need improvement.

## Cybersecurity Coordination

- Cybersecurity requirements, controls, assessment expectations, and
  incident-response procedures are defined through project-level cybersecurity
  or systems engineering processes, not by this Software Development Plan.
- Software teams coordinate with the project cybersecurity owner to apply
  applicable requirements to repositories, dependencies, continuous integration
  and deployment mechanisms, credentials, network interfaces, logging, and
  operational software.
- Software designs and releases identify security-relevant assumptions or
  dependencies where they affect architecture, interfaces, deployment, or
  operations.
- Cybersecurity findings that require software changes are tracked through the
  selected software issue-tracking process, with escalation to project-level
  risk management or change control when warranted.
- Detailed security control selection, threat analysis, authorization,
  vulnerability management policy, and incident-response procedures are owned by
  the responsible cybersecurity lead or team.

## Transition to Operations and Software Maintenance

- Software transition-to-operations planning will mature with the ngGONG
  operations concept, commissioning plan, site deployment model, and staffing
  model.
- Software delivered for operations should include the documentation, build
  records, release records, configuration information, verification evidence,
  and known-issue records needed to support operational use and maintenance.
- Operational software should provide appropriate observability, including logs,
  status, health information, metrics, alarms, or diagnostics needed for
  troubleshooting and maintenance.
- Software maintenance planning should address defect correction, dependency
  updates, interface changes, security updates, configuration changes, and
  compatibility with deployed hardware, site systems, and data-processing
  environments.
- Transition planning should identify which software components are maintained
  by ngGONG staff, contractors, vendors, or operations personnel.
- Operations-facing software should support controlled update, rollback,
  recovery, and configuration-management practices appropriate to its role and
  risk.
- Lessons learned from integration, commissioning, and early operations should
  feed back into requirements, design, tests, documentation, and maintenance
  priorities.
